q: In simple harmonic motion, the phase of the vibrating particle at an instant tells us its:
o: Maximum displacement from the mean position
Number of vibrations completed each second
Position and direction of motion at that instant
x: Phase (the angle ωt + φ) fixes where the particle is in its cycle and which way it is moving at that moment. The maximum displacement is the amplitude and vibrations per second is the frequency.

q: A particle performs SHM with a period of 0.5 s. Its angular frequency is:
x: ω = 2π/T = 2π/0.5 = 4π rad s⁻¹ (check: f = 2 Hz, ω = 2πf = 4π). Multiplying 2π by T instead of dividing gives π rad s⁻¹.

q: The displacement of a particle is x = 0.04 sin(10πt), with x in metres and t in seconds. The amplitude and frequency of its motion are:
x: Comparing with x = x₀ sin ωt: x₀ = 0.04 m and ω = 10π rad s⁻¹, so f = ω/2π = 5 Hz. Reading ω or the number 10 as the frequency gives the other values; 0.08 m is the peak-to-peak distance.

q: A particle performs SHM with amplitude 0.02 m and frequency 5 Hz. The magnitude of its maximum acceleration is:
x: ω = 2πf = 10π rad s⁻¹ and a_max = ω²x₀ = 100π² × 0.02 = 2π² m s⁻² (about 20 m s⁻²). 0.2π m s⁻¹ is ωx₀, the maximum speed; using f² x₀ without 2π gives 0.5.

q: A particle in SHM has a period of 1.2 s and starts from its mean position. The least time it takes to reach a displacement equal to half its amplitude is:
x: x = x₀ sin ωt with x = x₀/2 gives sin ωt = ½, so ωt = π/6 and t = T/12 = 0.1 s. Assuming constant speed (half of T/4) gives 0.15 s; 0.3 s is the time to reach the full amplitude.

q: Two particles P and Q perform SHM along parallel lines with the same amplitude and frequency. Whenever P is at its positive extreme, Q is at its negative extreme. The phase difference between them is:
x: Opposite extremes at the same instant means they are half a cycle apart, a phase difference of π rad. π/2 would put Q at its mean position when P is at an extreme; 2π means in phase.

q: A particle performs SHM of amplitude 3 cm and period 2 s. What total distance does it travel in 5 s?
x: 5 s is 2.5 periods. In each full period it travels 4 × amplitude = 12 cm, and in any half period 2 × amplitude, so the distance = 2 × 12 + 6 = 30 cm. Counting only 2 × amplitude per period gives 15 cm.

q: A particle performs SHM of amplitude x₀. At what distance from the mean position is its speed half of its maximum speed?
x: v = ω√(x₀² − x²) and v_max = ωx₀. Setting v = ωx₀/2 gives x₀² − x² = x₀²/4, so x = (√3/2)x₀ ≈ 0.87x₀. Assuming the speed falls linearly with distance gives x₀/2.

q: A seconds pendulum is a simple pendulum whose time period is:
x: A seconds pendulum takes 1 s for each swing from one extreme to the other, so a complete oscillation (there and back) takes 2 s. Taking one swing as the full period gives 1 s.

q: The length of a simple pendulum is increased by 44%. Its time period increases by:
x: T ∝ √l, so the new period is √1.44 = 1.2 times the old one: an increase of 20%. Taking T ∝ l gives 44%; halving 44% (the small-change approximation used for a large change) gives 22%.

q: The bob of a simple pendulum, of mass m, is displaced so that the string makes an angle θ with the vertical. The force that pulls the bob back towards its mean position is:
x: Resolve the weight: mg cos θ acts along the string (balanced, with the centripetal part, by the tension) and mg sin θ acts along the arc towards the mean position. This tangential part is the restoring force.

q: A simple pendulum moves with simple harmonic motion only when its amplitude is small, because only then:
o: The tension in the string equals the weight of the bob
Air resistance on the bob can be ignored
The string stays straight and does not stretch
sin θ ≈ θ (in radians), so the restoring force is proportional to the displacement
x: The restoring force is mg sin θ. Only for small θ is sin θ ≈ θ = x/l, giving F = −(mg/l)x, which is the SHM condition F ∝ −x. Tension and air resistance do not decide whether the motion is SHM.

q: A mass hung from a spring stretches it by 25 cm at rest. It is then set into small vertical oscillations. A simple pendulum with the same time period has a length of:
x: At rest mg = ke, so m/k = e/g and the spring's period is T = 2π√(m/k) = 2π√(e/g). A pendulum has T = 2π√(l/g), so l = e = 25 cm (both about 1 s).

q: A mass–spring system has period T when it oscillates horizontally on a smooth table. When the same mass hangs from the same spring and oscillates vertically, its period is:
x: T = 2π√(m/k) depends only on the mass and the spring constant, not on g. Gravity only shifts the mean position downward by mg/k, so the period is still T.

q: When a body in SHM passes through its mean position, its energy is:
x: At the mean position the displacement is zero, so the potential energy ½kx² is zero and the speed is greatest: all the energy is kinetic. At the extremes it is all potential.

q: A 0.1 kg mass performs SHM with angular frequency 20 rad s⁻¹ and amplitude 0.05 m. Its total energy is:
x: E = ½mω²x₀² = ½ × 0.1 × 400 × 0.0025 = 0.05 J (check: v_max = ωx₀ = 1 m s⁻¹ and ½mv² = 0.05 J). Forgetting the ½ gives 0.1 J; not squaring ω gives 0.0025 J.

q: A mass on a spring oscillates with amplitude x₀. It is replaced by a mass four times as large on the same spring, oscillating with the same amplitude x₀. Compared with before:
o: The total energy is the same and the maximum speed is unchanged
The total energy is four times as large and the maximum speed is unchanged
The total energy is the same and the maximum speed is halved
The total energy is the same and the maximum speed is doubled
x: Total energy = ½kx₀² depends only on k and x₀, so it is unchanged. Then ½mv_max² is the same, so v_max ∝ 1/√m and quadrupling m halves it (check: ω = √(k/m) halves, v_max = ωx₀).

q: A 0.2 kg mass on a spring performs SHM with amplitude 0.1 m. Its maximum speed is 1 m s⁻¹. The spring constant is:
x: Energy: ½kx₀² = ½mv_max², so k = mv²/x₀² = 0.2 × 1/0.01 = 20 N m⁻¹ (check: ω = v/x₀ = 10 rad s⁻¹ and k = mω² = 20 N m⁻¹). Not squaring the amplitude gives 2 N m⁻¹; 10 is ω.

q: At the instant when a particle in SHM moves at half its maximum speed, what fraction of its total energy is potential energy?
x: KE ∝ v², so at half the maximum speed KE = ¼ of the total energy; the rest, 3/4, is potential energy. 1/4 is the kinetic share, the usual mix-up.

q: An oscillating system is displaced and left to vibrate on its own, with no damping and no driving force. It vibrates:
o: At its natural frequency with steadily falling amplitude
At a frequency that steadily falls
At its natural frequency with constant amplitude
x: These are free oscillations: the system vibrates at its own natural frequency, and with no damping no energy is lost, so the amplitude stays constant. A falling amplitude would mean damping.

q: A microwave oven heats food mainly because:
o: The microwaves heat the metal walls, which then conduct heat to the food
The microwaves become hotter as they are reflected back and forth
The microwaves set up sound waves that rub the food
The microwaves make water molecules in the food vibrate strongly by resonance, so they absorb energy
x: The microwave frequency matches a natural frequency of the water molecules, so they absorb energy strongly (resonance) and the food warms from inside. The metal walls only reflect the microwaves.

q: The amplitude of a real oscillating system dies away gradually. This damping is caused by:
o: The restoring force, which always pulls it back to the mean position
Resistive forces such as friction and air resistance, which turn its mechanical energy into heat
A periodic driving force at its natural frequency
The inertia of the moving mass
x: Damping is the loss of mechanical energy to resistive (frictional) forces, which turn it into heat, so the amplitude decreases. The restoring force and inertia cause the oscillation itself; a driving force at the natural frequency would increase the amplitude.

q: Several pendulums of different lengths hang from one taut horizontal string. A heavy pendulum 60 cm long hanging from the same string is set swinging. After a while, the pendulum that swings with the largest amplitude is the one:
x: The heavy pendulum drives all the others at its own frequency. The one whose natural frequency matches, the pendulum of the same length (T = 2π√(l/g)), is in resonance and swings most. Bob mass does not set a pendulum's natural frequency.

q: The suspension of a car has a natural frequency of 1.5 Hz. The car is driven along a road with small ridges evenly spaced 6 m apart. Its bouncing is greatest at a speed of:
x: The ridges drive the suspension at f = v/d. Resonance when v/6 = 1.5, so v = 9 m s⁻¹ (check: one ridge every 6/9 s = 0.67 s, the natural period). Dividing 6 by 1.5 gives 4 m s⁻¹.
